title: Unified Emulation and Prototyping: Pipedream or Reality? - Semiwiki
gist: Synopsys' 2026 EP-Ready architecture upgrade introduces software-defined switching between emulation (ZeBu) and FPGA prototyping (HAPS) on a single hardware platform in minutes rather than days, a capability neither Cadence's Palladium/Protium two-platform strategy nor Siemens' three-tier Veloce portfolio currently matches, aimed at eliminating over-provisioning and idle-capacity waste for designs up to ~24 billion gates as verification gate counts race past 100 billion.

insights.claim: Gate counts in leading-edge data-center compute and AI training designs have crossed 100 billion gates, while mainstream SoC designs range from one to twenty billion gates, and leading-edge datacenter designs are approaching one trillion transistors (roughly 250 billion gates) in a single multi-die package within this decade.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Establishes the scale trajectory driving demand for ever-higher-capacity hardware-assisted verification, a structural tailwind for HAV vendors as designs continue to grow.

insights.claim: Simulation alone cannot provide the throughput required to validate a modern SoC in a commercially viable timeframe, making hardware-assisted verification platforms increasingly indispensable as time-to-market windows compress.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Frames HAV (emulation + prototyping) capex as a non-discretionary line item for advanced chip design teams, not an optional tooling upgrade.

insights.claim: Synopsys' EP-Ready architecture, significantly enhanced in 2026 with software-defined dual-mode switching, lets a single hardware platform transition between high-performance emulation (ZeBu) and FPGA prototyping (HAPS) without physical reconfiguration, overturning a decade-old industry separation between the two product categories.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: A structural product innovation that could reshape HAV purchasing decisions industry-wide if adopted, since it directly attacks the capital inefficiency of the prior two-platform model.

insights.claim: Prior EP-Ready systems switched between emulation and prototyping by physically re-cabling the interconnect and installing prototyping interface cards, a process taking several days and therefore performed only at procurement or a major project pivot; the new architecture removes physical intervention entirely, with software-orchestrated switching completing in minutes and repeatable multiple times per day.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: The minutes-versus-days mode-switch speed is the crux of the innovation's practical value, enabling truly dynamic capacity reallocation rather than one-time procurement decisions.
insights.quote: a team can run emulation on Monday, switch to prototyping for high-speed I/O validation on Tuesday, and revert for regression closure on Wednesday.

insights.claim: EP-Ready uses a direct-connect, point-to-point FPGA interconnect architecture rather than routing signals through a central switch fabric as many traditional emulators do, reducing interconnect latency and dedicating full link bandwidth to each connected pair without arbitration overhead.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: The architectural choice trades scalability for raw performance -- important context for evaluating EP-Ready against competitors' switch-fabric-based systems on a technical basis.

insights.claim: Direct-connect topologies are constrained by cable length, typically reaching up to 4 racks; EP-Ready trades a limited top capacity of up to 24 billion gates for higher performance than FPGA-based emulation already provides over processor-based emulation, while Synopsys recommends its ZeBu Server 5 for designs requiring capacity scalability beyond 60 billion gates.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Defines the precise capacity ceiling (~24 BG) within which EP-Ready's unified value proposition applies -- above that, customers still need a dedicated high-capacity emulator, capping the addressable market for the dual-mode pitch.

themes.theme: Competitive landscape: Cadence and Siemens still run separate platforms

insights.claim: Cadence pursues a two-platform strategy unified by a shared compiler: the processor-based Palladium Z3 delivers debug-rich emulation at comparatively low execution speed, while the FPGA-based Protium provides higher-speed prototyping-class runs with lighter debug; the pair scales to tens of billions of gates but requires two distinct hardware architectures with a larger overall footprint than a single reconfigurable platform.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Establishes Cadence as maintaining a physically-separate two-box approach, the direct point of competitive contrast against Synopsys' unified EP-Ready platform.

insights.claim: Siemens offers a three-tier portfolio unified by a common OS and compiler -- Veloce Strato CS (a purpose-built emulator chip, not a commercial FPGA) for emulation, Veloce Primo CS for enterprise prototyping on commercial FPGAs, and Veloce proFPGA CS for software prototyping -- collectively spanning the EP-Ready use-case range but across a custom-silicon emulator plus two FPGA-based prototyping platforms, considerably more distinct hardware than a single reconfigurable EP-Ready system.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Confirms Synopsys is currently the only major HAV vendor offering true single-platform dual-mode reconfiguration, a potential competitive moat if the approach proves commercially favored.

themes.theme: Technical and financial advantages of consolidation

insights.claim: Running separate emulation and prototyping systems (the norm for both Cadence and Siemens) duplicates recurring operational overhead -- power distribution, cooling infrastructure, network/system-management interfaces, and rack space -- per platform, whereas EP-Ready folds both functions onto one physical platform so this overhead is provisioned once.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Infrastructure consolidation is a direct operating-cost and lab/data-center-space savings argument that could sway budget-constrained customers toward EP-Ready over competing two-platform offerings.

insights.claim: In a conventional two-platform environment, hardware utilization is tied to the verification phase -- emulation dominates pre-silicon RTL closure while prototyping dominates embedded software validation -- so teams routinely find one platform oversubscribed while the other sits idle, with that idle capacity unable to be repurposed; EP-Ready removes this inefficiency by letting a single investment track the project's evolving needs with no additional purchase.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Utilization inefficiency in the legacy two-platform model is the core economic pain point EP-Ready targets, directly translatable into effective capacity/dollar improvement for adopting customers.

insights.claim: At the time of an HAV capacity purchase, budget owners cannot know what emulation/prototyping split will prove optimal over the system's five-year depreciation life, so in a two-platform world they hedge by over-provisioning both, and the excess capacity depreciates whether or not it is ever used; EP-Ready removes the guess by letting the buyer size total capacity once and let the mode split follow the project.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Frames EP-Ready as directly reducing capital-allocation risk over a 5-year depreciation horizon -- a quantifiable procurement-decision argument for CFOs and engineering budget owners evaluating HAV purchases.

themes.theme: Market re-segmentation and niche high-speed use cases

insights.claim: For the large majority of designs, the pre-installed dual-mode cabling delivers sufficient performance, but a narrower class -- where interface logic under test fits within one or two FPGAs (on the order of 120 million gates) -- benefits from optimized, direct point-to-point cable connections that can raise the prototype clock above 100 MHz, well beyond the platform's baseline, mattering for at-speed validation of interfaces such as USB high-speed links (480 Mbps).
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific niche (small, high-speed interface validation) where dedicated prototyping still outperforms EP-Ready's flexible baseline, useful for segmenting which customers remain best served by dedicated systems.

insights.claim: The EP-Ready architecture does not make dedicated emulation and prototyping systems obsolete; it changes the purchasing decision for the up-to-23-billion-gate HAV market by allowing organizations to trade some peak specialization for greater flexibility, utilization, and capital efficiency.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: A measured, non-promotional conclusion from the author: EP-Ready is a genuine architectural advance for a bounded segment of the market, not a wholesale replacement for high-capacity dedicated HAV systems -- useful framing for assessing Synopsys' realistic addressable opportunity.
